note: What this package asserts about where a coprocessor answers, and where each assertion comes from. Nintendo's Book II prints the two DSP windows; nothing a manufacturer printed covers the others, so every one of those names the evidence it does have and says plainly that it is not a document.

order: Nintendo's development manual, Book II, for the two DSP windows its Figures 3-1-4 and 3-1-5 print
the cartridge, because a driver was written by somebody who had the part on a desk and had to make it work
agreement across cartridges, because one driver could be wrong and thirty six agreeing could not be wrong the same way
authority.why: Most of these parts have no surviving datasheet, and the emulators that talk to them were written by people who read the same cartridge code this package reads. Taking a window from an emulator would be taking somebody's reading of the evidence rather than the evidence.
authority.whatIsMissing: A document for any window but the DSP's. Book I documents the memory map and the header and not the address lines a cartridge board decodes for a coprocessor; Book II prints the DSP-1's two windows and no other part's. Nothing printed by Seta or by Nintendo for the ST010, ST011, ST018 or OBC1 is known.

comparedAgainst.what: The driver routine of every cartridge in the manifest, disassembled out of the cartridge's own code.

windows.evidence: Read out of the driver routine of the Seta cartridges in the manifest.
windows.howToSettleIt: A Seta document, of which none is known, or a continuity reading across a real board.

windows.evidence: Read out of the driver routine of the Seta cartridges in the manifest. With the port window alone each ST010 cartridge yields one exchange; with this one they yield eighteen across eight shapes, and the Japanese and American releases agree on every shape. The bounds are the whole four kilobytes because the routines reach as far as 0x0FD5, and the control pair sits inside that rather than after it.
windows.howToSettleIt: A Seta document, of which none is known, or a continuity reading across a real board.
windows.selectedBy: One address line, named by selectBit.

windows.evidence: Read out of the driver routine of the one cartridge that carries this part. Inside the eight kilobytes it answers in, that cartridge reaches exactly 0x7FF0 through 0x7FF3 and 0x7FF6, which is the register set the model of the part declares, and the American and European releases agree. This is the cartridge saying where the registers are rather than an emulator saying it.
windows.howToSettleIt: A Nintendo application note naming the part, or a continuity reading across a real board.
windows.selectedBy: Not one line. The register file is the top sixteen bytes of an eight kilobyte window, so the decode is the top nine address lines being all ones rather than a single line going high the way it does on the other two parts.

windows.evidence: Read out of the driver routines of the one cartridge that carries this part, by a reachability walk from its reset vector rather than by the search this package uses for the others: every access is absolute, and this package only recognises a long one. Five routines in bank 0x00 are the whole of the console side, at file offsets 0x006717, 0x006862, 0x006873, 0x00687E and 0x006892, and between them they reach 0x3800, 0x3802 and 0x3804 and no other address in the window.
windows.howToSettleIt: A Nintendo application note naming the part, or a continuity reading across a real board. The bank range in particular is the one the other LoROM parts decode rather than one this cartridge establishes: every access observed executes in bank 0x00.
windows.selectedBy: Address bit 2, which is high for the status byte and low for the two data bytes. Bit 1 picks between the two data bytes underneath it, one the console reads and one it writes, so the three addresses are two lines rather than one.

decode.claim: A cartridge decodes a few address lines rather than all of them, so every address in the span reaches the same register and the part answers across a window rather than at one address.
decode.evidence: It follows from the windows above: the same part answers at 0x8000 under one layout and 0x6000 under another, and the line that picks between its two registers moves with the layout rather than staying with the part. A part that decoded its own address could not do that.
decode.howToSettleIt: A cartridge board schematic, or a continuity reading.

notStated: Which address lines any cartridge board actually connects for a part other than the DSP. Everything here about the ST010, ST011, ST018 and OBC1 is inferred from what the drivers do rather than read off a schematic or a manufacturer's figure.

Whether a window other than the DSP's extends past the addresses the drivers in the manifest reach. A driver shows where a part answers, never where it stops answering; Book II's figures give the DSP's whole span.
Anything about timing. How long the console spends on one of these accesses belongs to snes-mapper-python, and how long the part then runs belongs to snes-dsp-python.
Any part with no cartridge in the manifest. A window is only asserted where a driver was read.

partFromHeader.lowerNibble: *3H to *6H mark a co-processor; 00H, 01H and 02H mark none.
partFromHeader.readFrom: The text layer, which carries the table cell by cell, checked against the page image.

customChipBySubNumber.evidence: Book I prints what the cartridge type sub-number at FFBFH is for, distinguishing games of one cartridge type, and no values. Read out of the four custom-chip cartridges in the manifest: the two ST010 cartridges and the ST011 cartridge carry F6H with sub-number 01H, and the ST018 cartridge carries F5H with 02H.
customChipBySubNumber.howToSettleIt: A Nintendo or Seta list of the sub-numbers it assigned.
